passage:
"Not so close, Harish," said Parul, laughing, at the bus stop in Surat. Harish, five, leaned right into her face to show a beetle in his palm.
"It's big!"
"It is! But let's take one step back so I can see it. About an arm's length." She stretched out an arm. Harish stepped back until his fingers nearly touched it.
"Like that?"
"Perfect. Grandma gets a closer look though, right?"
"Yes, Grandma gets a hug." He grinned, and went to find the beetle a leaf.

qa.a: There was a big beetle in his palm.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling as he leaned into Parul's face?
qa.a: He was probably excited and eager to share his discovery, which is why he got so close. He probably wasn't trying to bother her.

qa.q: What made Parul's way of teaching personal space work?
qa.a: She explained it kindly with an arm's length and a clear example, and said some people such as Grandma can stand closer.

qa.q: How might Parul feel when Harish leans right into her face?
qa.a: She may feel a little crowded, though she stays friendly and gives him a clear guide.

grounding: A child learns that arm's length is a fair distance for many talks and that family may stand closer.

passage: Class note by Mridul, Reception teacher in Jaipur. Sumit, five, stands very close to friends when he speaks, so close that Aarav shrinks back. Today I knelt beside Sumit and said, "Let's find the right distance. Hold out your arm. That's the space where we usually talk." Then I asked him to practise with me. He stepped back, and beamed. Later, in a crowded queue, another child, Neel, froze and clutched his bag. I've taught the class to say, "Please give me space." Neel used it, and children moved back.

qa.q: How did Mridul teach Sumit the right distance?
qa.a: Mridul asked Sumit to hold out his arm and showed him that this is the space where we usually talk.

qa.q: What might Neel have been feeling when he froze in the crowded queue?
qa.a: He was probably uncomfortable at being crowded, since he clutched his bag. He might also have been unsure how to speak up.

qa.q: What could Mridul do to keep helping both children?
qa.a: Mridul can keep practising the arm's length and the sentence "Please give me space" with the whole class.

qa.q: How might Aarav feel when Sumit stands too close?
qa.a: Aarav may feel uncomfortable and want to move away, so the clear words help Aarav too.

grounding: A child learns arm's length is a fair distance, and children who crowd or freeze need gentle coaching and clear words.
